title: Transforming one coordinate world into another

blocks.text: Metric map production created a large coordinate-conversion job. W. I. Reilly published the New Zealand Map Grid design in 1973. The grid was used for the new 1:50,000 NZMS260 topographic series; its first sheet, T12 Thames, appeared in 1977. NZMG used NZGD49 as its underlying datum.
blocks.markdown: Metric map production created a large coordinate-conversion job. W. I. Reilly published the New Zealand Map Grid design in 1973. The grid was used for the new 1:50,000 NZMS260 topographic series; its first sheet, T12 Thames, appeared in 1977. NZMG used NZGD49 as its underlying datum.

blocks.text: Reilly’s projection used a distinctive polynomial expression tailored to keep scale distortion low across New Zealand. That local fit served national mapping well, but the mathematics was less familiar to general-purpose mapping software. When loading historic NZMS260 data, specify the source CRS explicitly rather than guessing from the coordinate values.

blocks.text: A projection change and a datum transformation are different operations. For a GIS practitioner restoring historic coordinates, record both the original grid and the transformation used, then compare the result against known control.

blocks.text: LINZ warns that transformation from NZMG to NZGD2000 is not straightforward. Keep the source coordinate values and the transformation record with the converted dataset so that its position can be checked and reproduced later.
